prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: Having read all eight openings, B028 is the candidate that most of the committee can support on its merits: six members rank it and four place it in their top three, including two first places. It has what I ask of any discovery: a clear theoretical idea (the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall proposal of Kane and Mele), an independent experimental confirmation in a different laboratory (Molenkamp's HgTe edge-transport measurement), and two decades of reproduction across many materials and techniques, including ARPES. The physics has lasted and has been used well beyond the original systems. The Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio pairs the decisive theory with the first decisive experiment, which is the pattern that has worked for the Academy. I rank B005 first on my own ballot, because I can judge an instrument-driven opening of a new observational window with confidence, but I only have two supporters there and I should not push my own field at the expense of what the committee can actually agree on. Condensed matter is outside my expertise, so I rely on the condensed-matter members for the physics and use my own experience only to test the evidence chain: prediction, independent measurement, reproduction.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary is the real weakness. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment actually tested, and none of them is in the supplied names. Hasan's ARPES discovery of 3D topological insulators is a separate and independently decisive step that a three-person limit forces us to leave out, so a citation that speaks only of the 2D quantum spin Hall effect may look incomplete to the community. There is also the argument that this follows the 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions too closely. Finally, if we pick B028 we leave aside B005, where a new window on the Universe was opened and the discovery claim is cleaner in the sense of nature giving an unexpected answer, although the credit there rests on a single name and a very large collaboration.

responses.point: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible trio but not unique; Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and Hasan's 3D work are the other natural claims, and the field is mature and overdue.
responses.response: I agree that the trio is defensible and not unique, and that is why I would write the citation around the two things the trio can claim without dispute: the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation. That avoids a statement about all topological insulators that Hasan and the 3D theorists could rightly contest. I do not think the missing BHZ prediction should block the prize, because the Kane-Mele proposal came first and stands on its own, but I would like you to say whether you think the committee should accept a trio that omits Hasan, or whether you would rather see the 3D strand handled by a second part.

responses.point: The Z2 mechanism is simple, general and rigorously analysable, extends the 2016 prize without duplicating it, and the right choice is the two theorists plus the first decisive experiment.
responses.response: I accept your argument and have adopted that configuration. The overlap with 2016 worries me a little more than it worries you: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological concepts, and a critic could say that this is a second bite. Your distinction, that the Z2 invariant with time-reversal symmetry is a different class of topological phase that does not need a magnetic field, is convincing to me as a non-specialist, but I would ask you to put it in a form we can write into the citation and defend externally.

responses.point: B005 is a clean discovery from nature that opened a new window on the Universe, with TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic-plane map as later support, though a solo award leaves credit questions.
responses.response: I put B005 first too, and I share your view that it is a real discovery with several independent channels and now KM3NeT as a cross-check. My difficulty is attribution, not physics: IceCube is a roughly 300-institution collaboration, AMANDA and the DUMAND and Baikal pioneers came before, and the supplied credit is one person, Halzen. A one-person prize for a collaboration-scale instrument would be the hardest of all the candidates to defend publicly, and the source classes beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 are still open. I therefore keep it as my first alternative to the preferred configuration rather than the preferred one, and I would ask whether you can see a defensible way to credit the pioneers beyond Halzen.

responses.point: B046 is first on her ballot: the 2018 correlated-insulator and superconductivity experiments are decisive, the flat-band prediction guided them, and Andrei's earlier STM work belongs to the record.
responses.response: I take the prediction-then-discovery argument seriously and I ranked B046 fourth. My reservation is maturity: the discovery is about eight years old and the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so I cannot yet tell whether the interpretation will last. The three-person limit also forces a choice among Andrei, Bistritzer and MacDonald that I cannot judge, and the order in which you put Andrei ahead of Bistritzer would need a careful reading of who did what first. I see it as a strong second choice, and in a later round I would like a clearer statement from the condensed-matter members on whether it is ready.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (B034) are the kind of measurement advance he values most: 10^-18 stability, tests of relativity and constants, and a coming redefinition of the second, with a clean two-name credit.
responses.response: I ranked B034 fifth and as an instrument builder I like the clean two-name credit and the independent confirmation in several laboratories. My concern is overlap with recent recognition: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered ion control, and I would want to hear from the atomic physicists whether the lattice clock is a new discovery or a very successful use of earlier prizes. I would not oppose it, but it has no more than three supporters on the committee, and the redefinition of the second, which would give it real weight, has not yet happened.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should credit only the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or also the 3D topological insulators (Hasan), and how to handle the BHZ prediction that is not in the supplied names.
Whether the topological theme sits too close to the 2016 prize for the committee's taste.
Whether a one-person prize for IceCube (B005) can be made acceptable, since I cannot assign credit beyond Halzen from the supplied names.
Whether the superconducting mechanism and other open questions make B046 premature, a judgment I defer to the condensed-matter members.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B028, B046 or B034. For B005, my own PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaboration work is in neighbouring astroparticle fields and I know the field, but I am not part of IceCube, so this is a professional familiarity and not a conflict that would require recusal; I note it so that the committee can weigh my enthusiasm for it accordingly.
